posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
When I dry Fuji material, after processing with Ascorbate developer and EDTA bleach, a strange effect happens:

Firstly all seems to be as normal. The hologram (exposed at 532nm) becomes brightly visible in red, then orange, then green, and then..... collapses and looses half of it's brightness.... 

Interestingly my first H2 hologram on this material did not do this and the hologram is very bright green. All subsequent ones were not as bright as the first one. I tried using fresh developer, changed beam ratios, changed exposure times, changed development times.... But never again the very pretty bright green hologram that I got on the first try....

posts.content_md:
I'm not sure about half loss but I've noticed a similar effect with all the emulsions I've used. The images are very much brighter wet than they are when fully dried.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I used the C315 for both the H1 and H2. Exposure time for the H2 was 1 second at 80uJ. This darkens the film in Ascorbate developer in about 5 seconds.

I am beginning to suspect now that it has to do with the bandwith of the film. 

For the very bright first hologram, the H1 was 5x7cm and the H2 of the same size. For all subsequent ones I made a new H1 master. The new H1 was as bright as the original, but much larger: 10x15cm. The new H2 were all of the original size (10x15cm). I did this to be able to have a much larger viewing angle for the H2's. I now suspect that the extra angular information that is recorded on the H2's that have been made from the larger H1 exceeds the bandwith of the film. Strangely though, H2's that were recorded on Ultimate 08 plates show the same lack of brightness as the H2's on FujiFilm.

Unfortunately I lost the original H1. I will try to block off the larger H1 to a size of 5x7cm to see if the new lack of angle information brings back the incredible brightness of the H2.

posts.author: MichaelH
posts.content_md:
Ahhh. I believe this is normal.

Several years ago Lon Moore recounted to several of us that he increased the brightness of his H2's by stopping down the H1 using a horizontal slit.

I've been doing this same thing since then with verifiable results. I typically use a cylinder lens to create the "slit" with the added benefit that I waste very little reconstruction light when making my H2's and so shorten my exposures.

By limiting vertical parallax to no more than you really need (most people don't jump up and down when looking at a hologram) you decrease the crosstalk and increase the final brightness.

Try putting a 5" high horizontal slit over your H1 and see if the final H2 is as bright as the original. I'll bet you a hologram that it will be.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: The master Lon was showing us was for a handheld hologram. For this only a small vertical parallax is needed. However on my holograms that are wall hung I find getting the geometry right so viewers of different heights quite challenging and I often use a larger slit than I can for a hand held hologram.

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md: Thank you for confirming my guess. I will give it a try for my next test. I can't wait to see my holograms bright again, but this time with a wide horizontal angle of view.

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
It sounds to me like there is shift in the fringe angle for the different parts of the H1. 

A simple test would be to take your lenses out of the reference beam. Then shine the raw laser at different parts (ie. center and the far four sides) and note the brightness of the real image on a white card. Maintain reference geometry by placeing a adjustable mirror at the point where the lens or spatial filter is so you can move the beam around the plate with the adjustable mirror while keeping the original reference angles the same for all part of the beam. 

If you want the center of your hologram the brightest. Find the angle where the raw beam through the middle creates the brightest real image on the card and use that angle no matter what the image brightness on the white card tells you when using the entire expanded beam.

Just my thoughts....

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Also, just for Ha-Ha's....

Illuminate your hologram with the entire reference beam and look at the real image floating in space through a polarizer and rotate the polarizer and see if anything weird is happening. You could flip the plate around and look at the virtual also the same way.

posts.author: Colin Kaminski
posts.content_md: Also, make sure you don't have any specular reflections at the film plane. Even a few mm away can eliminate burnout.
